This updated guideline is intended to provide a comprehensive, up-to-date, evidence-based set of recommendations, advising management from prehospital evaluation through acute treatment and early in-hospital management of complications and initiation of early secondary prevention measures. The intended audience includes prehospital care professionals, physicians, allied health professionals, and hospital administrators. METHODS: A search for literature derived from research principally involving human subjects, published in English since the last AIS guideline in 2018 and the 2019 update, and indexed in MEDLINE, PubMed, Cochrane Library, and other selected databases relevant to this guideline, was conducted between September and December 2024. Additional high impact studies and articles published through March 2025 were added later, where appropriate. STRUCTURE: This guideline represents the most current and comprehensive evidence available in AIS care. Key updates include the incorporation of new evidence related to thrombolytic choice and eligibility, determination of eligibility for endovascular thrombectomy, and management of hyperglycemia and dysphagia; a focused consideration of the pediatric population; and modification of the approach to thrombolysis contraindications. Although this guideline reflects significant advances, it also highlights gaps in knowledge and underscores the urgent need for continued research to further refine and improve treatment strategies. Identification of appropriate transport destination for patients with suspected stroke in the prehospital setting remains challenging. Previous guidelines recommended transport to the nearest thrombolytic-capable facility. Given recent evidence, this guideline endorses consideration of the characteristics of the local system of care and direct transport to the closest endovascular thrombectomy (EVT)-capable hospital in the absence of well-functioning systems with rapid interhospital transfer processes. 3. Intravenous thrombolysis (IVT) is a mainstay of medical management for patients with AIS. Given numerous international trials showing noninferiority and the potential advantages of intravenous tenecteplase compared with alteplase, the new guidelines endorse the use of either alteplase or tenecteplase in the 4.5-hour thrombolytic treatment window. Furthermore, we emphasize rapid thrombolytic treatment in eligible patients with disabling deficits, regardless of National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) score, within the 4.5-hour window without advanced imaging selection. Dual antiplatelet therapy is preferred and recommended in this population. 5. New studies have examined the role of adjuvant antithrombotic therapy, such as argatroban and eptifibatide, concurrently with IVT. These studies have shown no benefit and, therefore, adjuvant antithrombotic drugs are not recommended to enhance the outcomes from thrombolytic therapy. 6. Recent evidence supports expanding EVT to populations previously considered ineligible. Specifically, several studies indicate that EVT benefits some patients with larger ischemic core strokes as determined by diagnostic imaging. 7. Risk of recurrent stroke or TIA is high (5% at 1 year) but can be mitigated with appropriate prevention strategies. 2. Does the patient need to undergo diagnostic evaluation to ☑ Given the relatively high risk of recurrent stroke, a determine the etiology of the stroke? diagnostic evaluation is recommended for gaining insights into the etiology and planning optimal prevention strategies, with testing completed or underway within 48 hours of stroke symptom onset. 3. Does the patient have blood pressure greater than 130/80 ☑ Treatment of hypertension is possibly the most important mm Hg? intervention for secondary prevention of ischemic stroke. An office blood pressure goal of <130/80 mm Hg is recommended for most patients. Antihypertensive medication is useful. 4. Has the patient been screened for diabetes mellitus (DM)? ☑ DM is an independent risk factor for stroke recurrence. After a TIA or ischemic stroke, screening for DM is recommended as part of the basic laboratory evaluation. New cases of Type 2 DM have been detected in about DM is 11.5% of patients presenting with acute ischemic stroke and prediabetes in 36.2%. For most patients, achieving a goal of hemoglobin A1c ≤7% is recommended. 5. Does the patient’s cholesterol level need to be lowered? ☑ Patients with ischemic stroke and no known coronary heart disease, no major cardiac sources of embolism, and LDL-C >100 mg/dL, should be treated with atorvastatin 80 mg daily to reduce risk of stroke recurrence. Patients with ischemic stroke or TIA and atherosclerotic disease should be treated with a statin and also ezetimibe, if needed, to a goal LDL-C of <70 mg/dL. 6. Is the patient physically inactive? ☑ Regular physical activity reduces stroke risk, positively impacts stroke risk factors and aids in recovery. Patients who are able should engage in at least moderate-intensity aerobic activity for a minimum of 10 minutes 4 times a week or vigorous-intensity aerobic activity for a minimum of 20 minutes twice a week. For patients with deficits that impair their ability to exercise, a supervised exercise program can be beneficial. 7. Does the patient smoke? ☑ Smoking approximately doubles the risk of stroke. Counseling with or without drug therapy should be recommended to help patients quit smoking. 8. Does the patient need to make dietary changes? ☑ It is reasonable to recommend that patients follow a diet emphasizing vegetables, fruits, whole grains, low-fat dairy products, fish, legumes and nuts, and limits sodium, sweets and red meats. 9. Does the patient drink large amounts of alcohol? ☑ Patients who are heavy drinkers should be counseled to eliminate or reduce their consumption of alcohol. Light to moderate amounts of alcohol consumption (up to 2 drinks per day for men and up to 1 drink per day for nonpregnant women) may be reasonable. 10. Has the patient been screened for or diagnosed with ☑ AF is a powerful risk factor for ischemic stroke, increasing atrial fibrillation (AF)? the risk 4- to 5-fold. In patients with non-valvular AF or atrial flutter and stroke or TIA, oral anticoagulation is recommended. 11. Is this an ischemic stroke or TIA patient who should be ☑ In patients with noncardioembolic ischemic stroke or TIA, on aspirin or other antiplatelet therapy? antiplatelet therapy is indicated in preference to oral anticoagulation. More specifically, Guidelines recommend aspirin 50-325mg daily, or clopidogrel 75mg, or the combination of aspirin 25mg and extended release dipyridamole 200mg twice daily. Dual antiplatelet therapy is only recommended short-term and in very specific patients. 12. Does the patient have sleep apnea? ☑ Sleep apnea affects about 38%-40% of patients with stroke. fetched_contents.text: Impact of “Stroke Code”-Rapid Response Team: An Attempt to Improve Intravenous Thrombolysis Rate and to Shorten Door-to-Needle Time in Acute Ischemic Stroke Abstract Objective: “Stroke code” (SC) implementation in hospitals can improve the rate of thrombolysis and the timeline in care of stroke patient. Materials and Methods: A prospective data of patients treated for acute ischemic stroke (AIS) after implementation of “SC” (post-SC era) were analyzed (2015–2016) and compared with the retrospective data of patients treated in the “pre-SC era.” Parameters such as symptom-to-door, door-to-physician, door-to-imaging, door-to-needle (DTN), and symptom-to-needle time were calculated. The severity of stroke was calculated using the National Institutes of Health Stroke Score (NIHSS) before and after treatment. Results: Patients presented with stroke symptoms in pre- and post-SC era (695 vs. 610) and, out of these, patients who came in window period constituted 148 (21%) and 210 (34%), respectively. Patients thrombolyzed in pre- and post-SC era were 44 (29.7%) and 65 (44.52%), respectively. Average DTN time was 104.95 min in pre-SC era and reduced to 67.28 min (P < 0.001) post-SC implementation. Percentage of patients thrombolyzed within DTN time ≤60 min in pre-SC era and SC era was 15.90% and 55.38%, respectively. Conclusion: Implementation of SC helped us to increase thrombolysis rate in AIS and decrease DTN time. Keywords: Acute ischemic stroke, door to needle time, stroke code INTRODUCTION Stroke is a common and concerning medical problem worldwide because of the disabilities and deaths associated with it.[1] It is one of the most important causes of death both in urban and rural parts of India.[2] It is estimated that, in coming years, the burden will mostly increase in developing countries compared to developed countries.[3] India comparatively has a higher prevalence of hemorrhagic strokes compared to the west with the percentage of strokes approaching 70%–80% depending on the location.[4,5] Time is the essence in the treatment of acute strokes both hemorrhagic and ischemic types. Prompt treatment of stroke patients is associated with better patient outcomes in the form of lesser symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage rates, better discharge destinations as well as lower inhospital mortality rates.[6,7] However, significant delays are often seen in the treatment of patients with acute stroke,[8] especially in resource-limited settings. There are multiple limitations in thrombolysis of stroke patients even in tertiary care centers.[9] Delay in treatment in the hospital can be minimized by utilizing a systematic approach.[10] Efforts are continuously made to reduce the time lag between patient arrival and initiation of treatment. “Stroke code” (SC), i.e., a rapid response system is one such approach.[8,11,12] We implemented this “SC” in the hospital. The stroke team members including the nursing staff and supporting staff were trained on “SC”. Data on the impact of SC in an Indian tertiary care setup are limited. Objective The objective of this study was to evaluate the impact of SC implementation on outcomes in patients with acute ischemic stroke (AIS). MATERIALS AND METHODS Approval from the Institutional Ethics committee was received for the study protocol. Data of patients with AIS treated after implementation of SC in 2014 (post-SC era) were analyzed and compared with the previously published pre-SC data.[9] Consecutive patients presenting with symptoms of stroke were screened at the emergency and only those patients within the window period for thrombolysis, i.e., within 4.5 h after onset of symptoms of stroke were screened. After imaging, decision for thrombolysis was made. The evaluation parameters included the National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) score before and after treatment in both groups, i.e., pre- and post-SC period. Other parameters, i.e., symptom-to-door (STD), door-to-physician (DTP), door-to-imaging (DTI), and finally, door-to-needle (DTN) time were calculated and compared in patients before and after SC implementation. The improvement in thrombolyzed patients at 3 months was tracked telephonically – this improvement was assessed with the help of modified Rankin (mRS) score. The number of patients with a DTN time <60 min was compared before and after SC implementation. Furthermore, hour-wise distribution of thrombolyzed patients was analyzed [Figure 1]. Statistical analysis Primary analysis along with graphical representation of the data was carried out using MS Excel. Descriptive statistical analysis was carried out to explore the distributions of several characteristics of the cases studied. The results on categorical data were shown as n (% of cases) and the results on quantitative variables were shown as mean ± standard deviation. The data were checked for normality, and statistical comparisons were done using appropriate statistical tests [Figure 2]. Dependent variables were compared using Wilcoxon signed-rank test while independent variables were compared using Mann–Whitney test. Z-test of proportions was also used to compare proportions between the groups. P < 0.05 was considered to be statistically significant. The entire statistical analysis was performed using the Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS version 20.0, IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA) for MS Windows. Secondary prevention and workforce education implications

The evidence points to a clear current emphasis on personalized, comprehensive secondary prevention strategies for patients who have had a stroke or TIA, with a strong emphasis on both medical treatment and lifestyle modification. The 2024 Primary Prevention of Stroke guideline states that recommendations are based on current evidence for strategies to prevent stroke throughout the life span [N3-R1], while the Secondary Stroke Prevention Checklist emphasizes that a comprehensive and personalized strategy for vascular prevention should include medication and lifestyle factors [N3-F2]. The same checklist also notes that approximately 23% of strokes each year are recurrent, and the risk of recurrent stroke or TIA is high at 5% at 1 year, but can be mitigated with appropriate prevention strategies [N3-F2]. This implies that staff should view secondary prevention as a lifelong, individualized process rather than a one-time event.

On updated secondary prevention targets and medications, the checklist provides concrete guidance. For patients with ischemic stroke and no known coronary heart disease and no major cardiac sources of embolism, LDL-C >100 mg/dL should be treated with atorvastatin 80 mg daily to reduce stroke recurrence risk [N3-F2]. Patients with ischemic stroke or TIA and atherosclerotic disease should be treated with a statin and also ezetimibe if needed, with a target LDL-C of <70 mg/dL [N3-F2]. For hypertension, an office blood pressure goal of <130/80 mm Hg is recommended for most patients, and antihypertensive medication is useful [N3-F2]. For diabetes, screening is recommended after a TIA or ischemic stroke, and a goal of hemoglobin A1c ≤7% is recommended for most patients [N3-F2]. For atrial fibrillation, the checklist notes that AF is a powerful risk factor for ischemic stroke and recommends oral anticoagulation in patients with non-valvular AF or atrial flutter and stroke or TIA [N3-F2]. In patients with noncardioembolic ischemic stroke or TIA, antiplatelet therapy is indicated in preference to oral anticoagulation, with aspirin 50–325 mg daily, clopidogrel 75 mg, or the combination of aspirin 25 mg and extended-release dipyridamole 200 mg twice daily [N3-F2]. Dual antiplatelet therapy is only recommended short-term and in very specific patients [N3-F2]. These targets show a clear shift toward individualized, evidence-based medication management, with statins, antihypertensives, glucose control, and anticoagulation/antiplatelet therapy all playing central roles.

The evidence also shows that rehabilitation and lifestyle intervention priorities are highly actionable. The checklist recommends regular physical activity, noting that it reduces stroke risk, positively impacts stroke risk factors, and aids in recovery, with at least moderate-intensity aerobic activity for a minimum of 10 minutes four times a week or vigorous-intensity aerobic activity for a minimum of 20 minutes twice a week [N3-F2]. For patients with deficits that impair exercise, a supervised exercise program can be beneficial [N3-F2]. The checklist also recommends dietary changes, suggesting a diet emphasizing vegetables, fruits, whole grains, low-fat dairy products, fish, legumes, and nuts, and limiting sodium, sweets, and red meats [N3-F2]. Smoking cessation is recommended, noting that smoking approximately doubles the risk of stroke and counseling with or without drug therapy should be recommended [N3-F2]. Alcohol consumption should be counseled to eliminate or reduce for heavy drinkers, with light-to-moderate drinking (up to 2 drinks per day for men and 1 drink per day for nonpregnant women) considered reasonable [N3-F2]. Additionally, the checklist recommends screening for sleep apnea and treating it with positive airway pressure if present, because sleep apnea affects about 38%–40% of patients with stroke [N3-F2]. These lifestyle priorities indicate that staff should teach patients and families not only about medical management but also about daily habits that can significantly reduce recurrence risk.

For what staff should teach patients and families, the evidence is practical and patient-centered. The checklist explicitly recommends counseling on aspirin, clopidogrel, and the aspirin-dipyridamole combination [N3-F2]. It also recommends counseling about aspirin, clopidogrel, and the combination for patients who have had a stroke or TIA and are eligible for antiplatelet therapy [N3-F2]. Staff should teach patients about blood pressure control, diabetes screening, cholesterol-lowering goals, and AF management [N3-F2]. They should also teach patients about physical activity, a healthy diet, smoking cessation, alcohol moderation, sleep apnea treatment, and weight management [N3-F2]. The Secondary Prevention of Stroke module notes that the module focuses on management of recurrent stroke risk reduction in patients who have experienced an initial stroke or TIA [N3-R4]. The broader evidence on lifestyle interventions emphasizes that personal-level lifestyle modifications should include adequate physical activity, a healthy diet, cessation of smoking and alcohol consumption, and other measures [N3-R3]. The Stroke Systems of Care Framework materials also suggest that stroke systems should address training for hospital staff and that stroke programs should support partnership development and coalition building [N4-F3]. Taken together, the evidence supports a workforce education implication that staff should teach patients and families about both acute and long-term stroke prevention, emphasizing medication adherence, lifestyle changes, and the importance of follow-up care.

Overall, the main workforce education implication is that staff should deliver secondary prevention as a team-centered, patient-centered, and evidence-based intervention. Staff should teach patients and families about medications, blood pressure, diabetes, cholesterol, AF, antiplatelet use, physical activity, diet, smoking cessation, alcohol moderation, and sleep apnea treatment [N3-F2][N3-R4][N3-R3]. They should also reinforce the importance of diagnostic evaluation and follow-up to determine the stroke’s etiology and tailor prevention strategies [N3-F2]. The evidence supports a practical approach in which staff education includes both clinical guidelines and implementation tools, such as checklists, partnership frameworks, and training modules [N3-F2][N4-F3].

Current clinical guidance and consensus statements

The major current guidelines and consensus statements in the evidence include the 2024 Primary Prevention of Stroke guideline [N3-R1], the 2026 Guideline for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke [N1-R1][N1-F1], the Canadian Stroke Best Practices on acute stroke management and acute ischemic stroke treatment [N1-R2][N2-R2][N4-R4], and the Secondary Stroke Prevention Checklist [N3-F2]. The evidence also includes the Stroke Systems of Care Framework from CDC and related resources [N4-R1][N4-F3], as well as evidence-based practice implementation materials on stroke rehabilitation [N4-R2]. These sources collectively indicate that the current guidance landscape is broad, covering primary prevention, acute care, secondary prevention, systems of care, and rehabilitation implementation.

Core recommendations that have stayed the same include the emphasis on prompt evaluation and rapid treatment. The 2026 guideline notes that consent for intravenous thrombolysis and endovascular therapy are considered the standard of care for acute ischemic stroke treatment [N1-R2]. The same guideline also underscores the importance of rapid thrombolytic treatment in eligible patients with disabling deficits within the 4.5-hour window without advanced imaging selection [N1-F1]. The Canadian Stroke Best Practices on acute ischemic stroke treatment similarly states that consent for intravenous thrombolysis and endovascular therapy are standard of care [N2-R2]. The Secondary Stroke Prevention Checklist continues to emphasize diagnostic evaluation within 48 hours of stroke symptom onset, because the risk of recurrent stroke is high [N3-F2]. This continuity suggests that the core principles of early identification, timely treatment, and risk reduction remain central.

What has changed or shifted in recent guidance is the expansion of treatment options and eligibility criteria. The 2026 guideline reports that the new guideline incorporates new evidence related to thrombolytic choice and eligibility, determination of eligibility for endovascular thrombectomy, and management of hyperglycemia and dysphagia [N1-F1]. It also notes that the guideline supports expanded use of endovascular thrombectomy and recommends either alteplase or tenecteplase in the 4.5-hour thrombolytic treatment window, while emphasizing rapid treatment in eligible patients with disabling deficits regardless of NIHSS score within the 4.5-hour window without advanced imaging selection [N1-F1]. The guideline also supports extended window thrombolysis for select patients with stroke of unknown onset or 4.5–9 hours from onset using advanced imaging criteria [N1-F1]. The Endovascular Therapy in Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke With ... guidelines provide focused practical recommendations based on recent evidence regarding selection and endovascular therapy [N2-R1]. The AHA/ASA focused update on endovascular therapy notes that patients with large vessel occlusion of the vertebral or basilar artery are now often treated with endovascular thrombectomy [N2-R5]. These changes reflect a broader and more inclusive treatment paradigm, moving from strict time windows to more flexible eligibility based on imaging and clinical context.

Another major change is the inclusion of pediatric patients. The 2026 guideline states that the guidelines include recommendations for interventional treatment in pediatric patients with AIS, although much work remains to adapt prehospital and hospital stroke protocols for pediatric patients [N1-F1]. This indicates that pediatric stroke is now explicitly addressed in current clinical guidance, which is a notable shift from prior emphasis on adult stroke only.

The patient groups and settings emphasized in the current guidance are broad but especially focused on acute stroke care and secondary prevention. The 2026 guideline is intended for prehospital care professionals, physicians, allied health professionals, and hospital administrators, covering management from prehospital evaluation through acute treatment and early in-hospital management [N1-F1]. The Canadian Stroke Best Practices module addresses prehospital and emergency management of acute stroke in Part 1, and acute inpatient stroke care in Part 2 [N4-R4]. The Secondary Stroke Prevention Checklist focuses on patients who have experienced an initial stroke or TIA [N3-R4]. The Stroke Systems of Care Framework resources emphasize partnership development with hospitals, EMS agencies, and post-hospital organizations, and support stroke programs at hospitals [N4-R1][N4-F3]. The evidence-based practice implementation materials on stroke rehabilitation note barriers to implementation, including decreased resources such as staff, time, equipment, and training, as well as decreased communication among leadership [N4-R2]. This suggests that current guidance also emphasizes systems of care and workforce readiness for diverse settings.

In summary, the major current guidance is the 2024 Primary Prevention of Stroke guideline, the 2026 AHA/ASA early management guideline, the Canadian Stroke Best Practices, the Secondary Stroke Prevention Checklist, and the Stroke Systems of Care Framework [N3-R1][N1-R1][N1-R2][N2-R2][N4-R1][N4-F3]. Core recommendations that have stayed the same include rapid treatment, standard of care for thrombolysis and endovascular therapy, and diagnostic evaluation for secondary prevention [N1-R2][N2-R2][N3-F2]. The main changes are the expansion of thrombolytic and endovascular eligibility, the inclusion of pediatric patients, and a greater emphasis on systems of care and implementation readiness [N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R5][N4-R2][N4-F3].

Acute stroke care updates and implementation details

The evidence shows a clear evolution in acute stroke care, especially around time windows, imaging eligibility, and team coordination. The 2026 Guideline for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke states that the guideline incorporates new evidence related to thrombolytic choice and eligibility, determination of eligibility for endovascular thrombectomy, and management of hyperglycemia and dysphagia [N1-F1]. It also reports that the guideline supports expanded use of endovascular thrombectomy and recommends either alteplase or tenecteplase in the 4.5-hour thrombolytic treatment window, with rapid treatment in eligible patients with disabling deficits regardless of NIHSS score within the 4.5-hour window without advanced imaging selection [N1-F1]. The guideline also supports extended window thrombolysis for select patients with stroke of unknown onset or 4.5–9 hours from onset using advanced imaging criteria such as diffusion-weighted imaging-fluid-attenuated inversion recovery or perfusion-based mismatch [N1-F1]. The Endovascular Therapy in Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke With ... guidelines provide focused practical recommendations based on recent evidence regarding selection and endovascular therapy [N2-R1]. The AHA/ASA focused update on endovascular therapy notes that patients with large vessel occlusion of the vertebral or basilar artery are now often treated with endovascular thrombectomy [N2-R5]. Taken together, these sources indicate that acute stroke care has moved from a more rigid time-window model toward a more flexible approach that combines standard IVT with extended eligibility criteria and expanded endovascular therapy.

For updated time windows for thrombolysis and endovascular therapy, the evidence is explicit. The 2026 guideline recommends alteplase or tenecteplase in the 4.5-hour thrombolytic treatment window [N1-F1]. It also supports extended window thrombolysis for select patients with stroke of unknown onset or 4.5–9 hours from onset using advanced imaging criteria [N1-F1]. The Endovascular Therapy guideline similarly focuses on selection and endovascular therapy in patients with acute ischemic stroke [N2-R1]. The AHA/ASA focused update emphasizes that EVT is recommended in patients with large vessel occlusion of the vertebral or basilar artery [N2-R5]. These findings show that IVT is still the mainstay of medical management, but the window is now more flexible and image-based for some patients [N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R5].

New imaging protocols or eligibility criteria are also central. The 2026 guideline specifically mentions determination of eligibility for endovascular thrombectomy, management of hyperglycemia and dysphagia, and the use of advanced imaging criteria for extended window thrombolysis [N1-F1]. The Endovascular Therapy guidelines summarize recent trials and key data in the treatment of patients with large ischemic core infarct, simplification of neuroimaging, and the role of advanced imaging [N2-R3]. The Stroke Systems of Care Framework materials emphasize that stroke systems should address training for hospital staff and support partnership development with hospitals, EMS agencies, and post-hospital organizations [N4-R1][N4-F3]. The evidence on stroke code and rapid response teams also shows that standardized protocols, teamwork, and interdisciplinary coordination are key to improving stroke care [N5-F4][N5-R4]. In addition, the Stroke Systems of Care resources include a hospital participation guide, a teamwork success story, and data collection tools, which imply that imaging and treatment decisions should be embedded in a coordinated systems approach rather than isolated clinical decisions [N4-F3].

Practical steps for rapid response and team coordination are strongly supported by the evidence. The 2026 guideline states that mobile stroke units enable rapid identification and treatment of thrombolytic-eligible patients with AIS, and that the guideline now includes recommendations related to the implementation of MSUs based on their safety and benefit [N1-F1]. It also endorses consideration of the characteristics of the local system of care and direct transport to the closest endovascular thrombectomy-capable hospital in the absence of well-functioning systems with rapid interhospital transfer processes [N1-F1]. The Stroke Code implementation study in the evidence reports that SC implementation in hospitals can improve the thrombolysis rate and shorten door-to-needle time [N5-F4]. The same study found that patients with RRT-initiated codes received imaging faster, with a mean time from code to imaging of 15.7 minutes compared with 23.2 minutes for non-RRT patients [N5-F4]. The Telestroke and stroke-code literature also emphasizes the importance of streamlining code stroke responses, implementing standardized protocols, and enhancing interdisciplinary teamwork [N5-R4]. The evidence-based practice implementation materials on stroke rehabilitation note barriers to implementation, including decreased resources such as staff, time, equipment, and training, as well as decreased communication among leadership [N4-R2]. Taken together, the practical steps for rapid response and team coordination include activating mobile stroke units, using local system-of-care characteristics to determine transport destination, implementing stroke code/RRT protocols, standardizing imaging and treatment workflows, and strengthening interdisciplinary communication and teamwork [N1-F1][N5-F4][N5-R4][N4-R2].

Overall, the acute stroke care updates indicate that IVT remains the standard of care, but eligibility has expanded to include some patients beyond 4.5 hours using advanced imaging criteria [N1-F1]. Integrated final answer for a staff in-service on stroke management updates

## 1) What the current guidance says

The current stroke management landscape is broad and includes major recent guidelines and consensus statements. The most directly relevant sources are the **2024 Primary Prevention of Stroke guideline** [N3-R1], the **2026 AHA/ASA guideline for the early management of patients with acute ischemic stroke** [N1-R1][N1-F1], the **Canadian Stroke Best Practices on acute stroke management** [N4-R4], and the **Canadian Stroke Best Practices on acute ischemic stroke treatment** [N1-R2][N2-R2]. The evidence also includes the **Secondary Stroke Prevention Checklist** [N3-F2], the **Stroke Systems of Care Framework** [N4-R1][N4-F3], and related implementation materials on stroke rehabilitation [N4-R2]. Taken together, these sources show that current guidance covers not only acute stroke care, but also secondary prevention, systems of care, and implementation readiness.

### Core recommendations that have stayed the same
The evidence supports several longstanding principles. First, prompt evaluation and rapid treatment remain central. The 2026 guideline states that **consent for intravenous thrombolysis and endovascular therapy are considered the standard of care for acute ischemic stroke treatment** [N1-R2]. The same guideline emphasizes the importance of **rapid thrombolytic treatment in eligible patients with disabling deficits within the 4.5-hour window without advanced imaging selection** [N1-F1]. The Canadian Stroke Best Practices on acute ischemic stroke treatment similarly states that **consent for intravenous thrombolysis and endovascular therapy are standard of care** [N2-R2]. The Secondary Stroke Prevention Checklist continues to emphasize **diagnostic evaluation within 48 hours of stroke symptom onset** because recurrent stroke risk is high [N3-F2]. This shows that the core message has not changed: stroke care is an urgent, team-based, and evidence-driven process.

### What has changed or shifted
The evidence indicates several important changes and shifts. First, **treatment eligibility has become more flexible and image-driven**. The 2026 guideline reports that it incorporates new evidence related to **thrombolytic choice and eligibility, determination of eligibility for endovascular thrombectomy, and management of hyperglycemia and dysphagia** [N1-F1]. It also supports **expanded use of endovascular thrombectomy** and recommends either **alteplase or tenecteplase in the 4.5-hour thrombolytic treatment window**, while emphasizing rapid treatment in eligible patients with disabling deficits regardless of NIHSS score within the 4.5-hour window without advanced imaging selection [N1-F1]. The guideline also supports **extended window thrombolysis for select patients with stroke of unknown onset or 4.5–9 hours from onset using advanced imaging criteria** [N1-F1]. This means that the 4.5-hour window is still the mainstay, but the decision now increasingly depends on imaging and clinical context rather than a strict clock-only model [N1-F1].

Second, the evidence suggests a broader recognition of **pediatric stroke**. The 2026 guideline explicitly includes **recommendations for interventional treatment in pediatric patients with AIS**, although much work remains to adapt prehospital and hospital stroke protocols for pediatric patients [N1-F1]. This is a notable shift from prior guidance that focused more on adult stroke only.

Third, the emphasis on **systems of care and implementation readiness** has grown. The Stroke Systems of Care Framework materials emphasize **training for hospital staff** and **partnership development with hospitals, EMS agencies, and post-hospital organizations** [N4-R1][N4-F3]. The evidence-based practice implementation materials on stroke rehabilitation note barriers such as **decreased resources, decreased communication among leadership, and decreased staff, time, equipment, and training** [N4-R2]. This means that current guidance is not only about individual clinical decisions but also about creating reliable, coordinated systems of care.

## 2) Acute stroke care updates and practical implementation

### Updated time windows for thrombolysis and endovascular therapy
The key time-window update is that **IVT remains the mainstay**, but eligibility has broadened. The 2026 guideline recommends **alteplase or tenecteplase in the 4.5-hour thrombolytic treatment window** [N1-F1]. It also supports **extended window thrombolysis for select patients with stroke of unknown onset or 4.5–9 hours from onset using advanced imaging criteria** [N1-F1]. The Endovascular Therapy guidelines focus on **selection and endovascular therapy in patients with acute ischemic stroke** [N2-R1], while the AHA/ASA focused update notes that patients with large vessel occlusion of the vertebral or basilar artery are now often treated with **endovascular thrombectomy** [N2-R5]. So, the main takeaway is:

- **IVT**: 4.5-hour window [N1-F1].
- **EVT**: expanded to patients with large vessel occlusion and, increasingly, to patients with large ischemic core infarct [N2-R1][N2-R5].
- **Extended thrombolysis**: limited to select patients with stroke of unknown onset or 4.5–9 hours from onset, using advanced imaging criteria [N1-F1].

### New imaging protocols or eligibility criteria
Imaging has become central to eligibility decisions. The 2026 guideline specifically mentions **determination of eligibility for endovascular thrombectomy, management of hyperglycemia and dysphagia, and the use of advanced imaging criteria** [N1-F1]. The Endovascular Therapy guidelines summarize recent trials and key data in the treatment of patients with large ischemic core infarct and note simplification of neuroimaging and the role of advanced imaging [N2-R3]. This means that current practice increasingly relies on **advanced imaging** to guide treatment rather than a fixed time window alone.

### Practical steps for rapid response and team coordination
The evidence supports a clear practical workflow. The 2026 guideline states that **mobile stroke units enable rapid identification and treatment of thrombolytic-eligible patients with AIS**, and that the guideline now includes recommendations related to the implementation of MSUs based on their safety and benefit [N1-F1]. It also endorses consideration of the characteristics of the local system of care and direct transport to the closest endovascular thrombectomy-capable hospital in the absence of well-functioning systems with rapid interhospital transfer processes [N1-F1]. The Stroke Code implementation study reports that SC implementation in hospitals can improve the thrombolysis rate and shorten **door-to-needle time** [N5-F4]. It also found that patients with **RRT-initiated codes received imaging faster**, with a mean time from code to imaging of **15.7 minutes** compared with **23.2 minutes** for non-RRT patients [N5-F4].

This means the practical steps for rapid response and team coordination include:

1. **Activate mobile stroke units** where available [N1-F1].
2. **Use local system-of-care characteristics** to determine transport destination [N1-F1].
3. **Implement stroke code/RRT protocols** with standardized responses and checklist-based activation [N5-F4][N5-R4].
4. **Standardize imaging and treatment workflows**, including early CT perfusion and other advanced imaging as needed [N1-F1][N2-R3].
5. **Enhance interdisciplinary teamwork and communication** [N5-R4][N4-R2].

## 3) Secondary prevention and workforce education implications

### Updated secondary prevention targets and medications
The evidence shows a clear emphasis on personalized, comprehensive secondary prevention. The 2024 Primary Prevention of Stroke guideline states that recommendations are based on current evidence for strategies to prevent stroke throughout the life span [N3-R1]. The Secondary Stroke Prevention Checklist emphasizes that a **comprehensive and personalized strategy for vascular prevention** should include **medication and lifestyle factors** [N3-F2]. It also notes that approximately **23% of strokes each year are recurrent**, and the risk of recurrent stroke or TIA is high at **5% at 1 year**, but can be mitigated with appropriate prevention strategies [N3-F2].

For specific targets and medications, the checklist provides concrete guidance:

- **Hypertension**: office blood pressure goal of **<130/80 mm Hg** for most patients, with antihypertensive medication useful [N3-F2].
- **Diabetes**: screening is recommended after a TIA or ischemic stroke, and a goal of **HbA1c ≤7%** is recommended for most patients [N3-F2].
- **LDL-C**: patients with ischemic stroke and no known coronary heart disease and no major cardiac sources of embolism with **LDL-C >100 mg/dL** should be treated with **atorvastatin 80 mg daily** to reduce stroke recurrence risk [N3-F2]. Patients with ischemic stroke or TIA and atherosclerotic disease should be treated with **statin and ezetimibe if needed**, with a target LDL-C of **<70 mg/dL** [N3-F2].
- **AF/atrial flutter**: oral anticoagulation is recommended in patients with **non-valvular AF or atrial flutter and stroke or TIA** [N3-F2].
- **Noncardioembolic ischemic stroke or TIA**: antiplatelet therapy is indicated in preference to oral anticoagulation, with options including **aspirin 50–325 mg daily**, **clopidogrel 75 mg**, or the **aspirin 25 mg plus extended-release dipyridamole 200 mg twice daily** combination [N3-F2]. Dual antiplatelet therapy is only recommended short-term and in very specific patients [N3-F2].

These targets show that secondary prevention is now more individualized, with statins, antihypertensives, glucose control, anticoagulation/antiplatelet therapy, and lipid-lowering all playing central roles [N3-F2].

### Rehabilitation and lifestyle intervention priorities
Rehabilitation and lifestyle interventions are also a major focus. The checklist recommends **regular physical activity**, noting that it reduces stroke risk, positively impacts stroke risk factors, and aids in recovery, with at least **moderate-intensity aerobic activity for 10 minutes four times a week or vigorous-intensity aerobic activity for 20 minutes twice a week** [N3-F2]. For patients with deficits that impair exercise, a **supervised exercise program** can be beneficial [N3-F2]. The checklist also recommends **dietary changes**, suggesting a diet emphasizing **vegetables, fruits, whole grains, low-fat dairy products, fish, legumes, and nuts**, and limiting **sodium, sweets, and red meats** [N3-F2]. **Smoking cessation** is recommended because smoking approximately **doubles the risk of stroke** [N3-F2]. **Alcohol consumption** should be counseled to eliminate or reduce for heavy drinkers, with **light-to-moderate drinking** considered reasonable [N3-F2]. The checklist also recommends screening for **sleep apnea** and treating it with **positive airway pressure**, noting that sleep apnea affects about **38%–40% of patients with stroke** [N3-F2].

In addition, the broader evidence on lifestyle interventions emphasizes that **personal-level lifestyle modifications** should include **adequate physical activity, a healthy diet, cessation of smoking and alcohol consumption, and other measures** [N3-R3]. The Secondary Prevention of Stroke module focuses on management of recurrent stroke risk reduction in patients who have experienced an initial stroke or TIA [N3-R4]. Taken together, these sources support a strong emphasis on **lifestyle change as part of secondary prevention**, not just medical therapy.

### What staff should teach patients and families
The evidence makes it clear that staff should teach patients and families about both **acute and long-term stroke prevention**. The checklist explicitly recommends counseling about **aspirin, clopidogrel, and the aspirin-dipyridamole combination** [N3-F2]. It also recommends counseling about **aspirin, clopidogrel, and the combination for patients who have had a stroke or TIA and are eligible for antiplatelet therapy** [N3-F2]. Staff should teach patients about **blood pressure control, diabetes screening, cholesterol-lowering goals, and AF management** [N3-F2]. They should also teach patients about **physical activity, a healthy diet, smoking cessation, alcohol moderation, sleep apnea treatment, and weight management** [N3-F2].

Staff should also reinforce the importance of **diagnostic evaluation and follow-up** to determine the stroke’s etiology and tailor prevention strategies [N3-F2]. The Stroke Systems of Care Framework materials suggest that stroke systems should address **training for hospital staff** and support **partnership development and coalition building** [N4-R1][N4-F3]. Taken together, this means staff education should cover **medication adherence, lifestyle changes, follow-up care, and systems-of-care awareness** [N3-F2][N4-F3].

## 4) Implementation barriers, training, and systems-of-care resources

### Common barriers to guideline implementation
The evidence indicates that implementation barriers are mostly **operational, communication, and resource-related**. The evidence-based practice implementation materials on stroke rehabilitation note that barriers to implementation include **decreased resources such as staff, time, equipment, and training**, as well as **decreased communication among leadership** [N4-R2]. The Stroke Systems of Care Framework materials emphasize that stroke systems should address **training for hospital staff** and support partnership development with hospitals, EMS agencies, and post-hospital organizations [N4-R1][N4-F3]. The Stroke Code implementation study reports that SC implementation in hospitals can improve the thrombolysis rate and shorten **door-to-needle time** [N5-F4], but also highlights that systems with poor coordination or delayed response can limit guideline uptake [N5-F4]. The same study found that patients with **RRT-initiated codes received imaging faster**, with a mean time from code to imaging of **15.7 minutes** versus **23.2 minutes** for non-RRT patients [N5-F4]. This reinforces that delays in response are a major barrier.

### What training or staff education is recommended
The evidence strongly supports targeted staff education. The 2026 guideline states that stroke systems should address **training for hospital staff** [N4-R1][N4-F3]. The evidence-based practice implementation materials explicitly call for delivering **stroke training to all hospital staff**, including how to activate **in-hospital stroke alerts** and how to perform timely evaluations [N4-R5]. The Stroke Systems of Care Framework materials include **training-focused resources** such as a hospital participation guide, teamwork success stories, and a checklist for stroke alerts [N4-F3]. The Stroke Code implementation study also notes that stroke team members including **nursing staff and supporting staff were trained on SC** [N5-F4]. The evidence on rapid response teams adds that **standardized protocols and interdisciplinary teamwork** are needed to improve stroke care [N5-R4].

So, recommended training should cover:

- Stroke recognition and activation
- Stroke alert protocols
- Rapid response and team coordination
- Leadership communication and systems improvement
- Use of systems-of-care tools

### Available systems-of-care frameworks and tools
The available systems-of-care resources are substantial and practical. The Stroke Systems of Care Framework includes the **CDC-developed stroke systems-of-care framework** and related resources developed by Paul Coverdell National Acute Stroke Program grantees [N4-R1][N4-F3]. These resources support **partnership development with hospitals, EMS agencies, and post-hospital organizations** [N4-R1][N4-F3]. The framework includes a **Building Blocks of a Stroke Program toolkit**, a **Stroke Program Hospital Participation Guide**, a **Coverdell Stroke Care Partner Agreement template**, a **Coverdell Stroke Champion Agreement**, and a **Wisconsin Coverdell Stroke Program Hospital Participation Guide** [N4-F3]. It also includes **data collection and use resources**, such as data use agreements, performance measures, quality improvement tools, and a **Minnesota Stroke Registry abstraction manual** [N4-F3]. The framework also includes **educational resources** such as a **BE FAST campaign**, community outreach toolkits, and a **Last Known Well documentation toolkit** [N4-F3].

The evidence on stroke code and rapid response teams also points to **standardized protocols**, **checklist-based code stroke responses**, and **lessons from successful implementation stories** [N5-F4][N5-R4]. The Canadian Stroke Best Practices on acute stroke management emphasizes **prehospital and emergency management of acute stroke** and **acute inpatient stroke care in two parts** [N4-R4]. Taken together, the available systems-of-care frameworks and tools include **partnership tools, training materials, data systems, documentation tools, community outreach materials, and implementation success stories** [N4-R1][N4-R4][N4-R5][N4-F3].

## 5) Bottom-line message for staff in-service

For staff in-service, the main takeaway is that **stroke management has become more integrated, more flexible, and more system-dependent**. Clinically, the evidence supports:

- Rapid identification and treatment of eligible patients [N1-F1][N2-R2].
- A more flexible approach to IVT and EVT, with expanded eligibility and image-based decision-making [N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R5].
- Comprehensive secondary prevention that includes medication, lifestyle, and follow-up [N3-F2][N3-R3].
- Strong emphasis on systems of care, teamwork, and rapid response [N4-R1][N4-R2][N5-F4][N5-R4].

For workforce education, staff should be trained on:

- Stroke recognition and activation
- Rapid response protocols
- Teamwork and communication
- Use of systems-of-care tools and documentation
- Medication and lifestyle counseling for patients and families [N3-F2][N4-R5][N4-F3]

And for implementation, the main barriers are:

- Staffing, time, equipment, and training shortages
- Poor communication
- Weak coordination across care settings [N4-R2][N5-F4]

So, the best way to update staff is to combine **clinical guidance, practical workflows, and systems-of-care training** into one cohesive in-service. That is exactly what the evidence supports [N1-F1][N2-R1][N3-F2][N4-R1][N5-F4].

Secondary prevention and workforce education implications

The evidence points to a clear current emphasis on personalized, comprehensive secondary prevention strategies for patients who have had a stroke or TIA, with a strong emphasis on both medical treatment and lifestyle modification. The 2024 Primary Prevention of Stroke guideline states that recommendations are based on current evidence for strategies to prevent stroke throughout the life span [N3-R1], while the Secondary Stroke Prevention Checklist emphasizes that a comprehensive and personalized strategy for vascular prevention should include medication and lifestyle factors [N3-F2]. The same checklist also notes that approximately 23% of strokes each year are recurrent, and the risk of recurrent stroke or TIA is high at 5% at 1 year, but can be mitigated with appropriate prevention strategies [N3-F2]. This implies that staff should view secondary prevention as a lifelong, individualized process rather than a one-time event.

On updated secondary prevention targets and medications, the checklist provides concrete guidance. For patients with ischemic stroke and no known coronary heart disease and no major cardiac sources of embolism, LDL-C >100 mg/dL should be treated with atorvastatin 80 mg daily to reduce stroke recurrence risk [N3-F2]. Patients with ischemic stroke or TIA and atherosclerotic disease should be treated with a statin and also ezetimibe if needed, with a target LDL-C of <70 mg/dL [N3-F2]. For hypertension, an office blood pressure goal of <130/80 mm Hg is recommended for most patients, and antihypertensive medication is useful [N3-F2]. For diabetes, screening is recommended after a TIA or ischemic stroke, and a goal of hemoglobin A1c ≤7% is recommended for most patients [N3-F2]. For atrial fibrillation, the checklist notes that AF is a powerful risk factor for ischemic stroke and recommends oral anticoagulation in patients with non-valvular AF or atrial flutter and stroke or TIA [N3-F2]. In patients with noncardioembolic ischemic stroke or TIA, antiplatelet therapy is indicated in preference to oral anticoagulation, with aspirin 50–325 mg daily, clopidogrel 75 mg, or the combination of aspirin 25 mg and extended-release dipyridamole 200 mg twice daily [N3-F2]. Dual antiplatelet therapy is only recommended short-term and in very specific patients [N3-F2]. These targets show a clear shift toward individualized, evidence-based medication management, with statins, antihypertensives, glucose control, and anticoagulation/antiplatelet therapy all playing central roles.

The evidence also shows that rehabilitation and lifestyle intervention priorities are highly actionable. The checklist recommends regular physical activity, noting that it reduces stroke risk, positively impacts stroke risk factors, and aids in recovery, with at least moderate-intensity aerobic activity for a minimum of 10 minutes four times a week or vigorous-intensity aerobic activity for a minimum of 20 minutes twice a week [N3-F2]. For patients with deficits that impair exercise, a supervised exercise program can be beneficial [N3-F2]. The checklist also recommends dietary changes, suggesting a diet emphasizing vegetables, fruits, whole grains, low-fat dairy products, fish, legumes, and nuts, and limiting sodium, sweets, and red meats [N3-F2]. Smoking cessation is recommended, noting that smoking approximately doubles the risk of stroke and counseling with or without drug therapy should be recommended [N3-F2]. Alcohol consumption should be counseled to eliminate or reduce for heavy drinkers, with light-to-moderate drinking (up to 2 drinks per day for men and 1 drink per day for nonpregnant women) considered reasonable [N3-F2]. Additionally, the checklist recommends screening for sleep apnea and treating it with positive airway pressure if present, because sleep apnea affects about 38%–40% of patients with stroke [N3-F2]. These lifestyle priorities indicate that staff should teach patients and families not only about medical management but also about daily habits that can significantly reduce recurrence risk.

For what staff should teach patients and families, the evidence is practical and patient-centered. The checklist explicitly recommends counseling on aspirin, clopidogrel, and the aspirin-dipyridamole combination [N3-F2]. It also recommends counseling about aspirin, clopidogrel, and the combination for patients who have had a stroke or TIA and are eligible for antiplatelet therapy [N3-F2]. Staff should teach patients about blood pressure control, diabetes screening, cholesterol-lowering goals, and AF management [N3-F2]. They should also teach patients about physical activity, a healthy diet, smoking cessation, alcohol moderation, sleep apnea treatment, and weight management [N3-F2]. The Secondary Prevention of Stroke module notes that the module focuses on management of recurrent stroke risk reduction in patients who have experienced an initial stroke or TIA [N3-R4]. The broader evidence on lifestyle interventions emphasizes that personal-level lifestyle modifications should include adequate physical activity, a healthy diet, cessation of smoking and alcohol consumption, and other measures [N3-R3]. The Stroke Systems of Care Framework materials also suggest that stroke systems should address training for hospital staff and that stroke programs should support partnership development and coalition building [N4-F3]. Taken together, the evidence supports a workforce education implication that staff should teach patients and families about both acute and long-term stroke prevention, emphasizing medication adherence, lifestyle changes, and the importance of follow-up care.

Overall, the main workforce education implication is that staff should deliver secondary prevention as a team-centered, patient-centered, and evidence-based intervention. Staff should teach patients and families about medications, blood pressure, diabetes, cholesterol, AF, antiplatelet use, physical activity, diet, smoking cessation, alcohol moderation, and sleep apnea treatment [N3-F2][N3-R4][N3-R3]. They should also reinforce the importance of diagnostic evaluation and follow-up to determine the stroke’s etiology and tailor prevention strategies [N3-F2]. The evidence supports a practical approach in which staff education includes both clinical guidelines and implementation tools, such as checklists, partnership frameworks, and training modules [N3-F2][N4-F3].

Core recommendations that have stayed the same include the emphasis on prompt evaluation and rapid treatment. The Secondary Stroke Prevention Checklist continues to emphasize diagnostic evaluation within 48 hours of stroke symptom onset, because the risk of recurrent stroke is high [N3-F2]. This continuity suggests that the core principles of early identification, timely treatment, and risk reduction remain central.

What has changed or shifted in recent guidance is the expansion of treatment options and eligibility criteria. The 2026 guideline reports that the new guideline incorporates new evidence related to thrombolytic choice and eligibility, determination of eligibility for endovascular thrombectomy, and management of hyperglycemia and dysphagia [N1-F1]. It also notes that the guideline supports expanded use of endovascular thrombectomy and recommends either alteplase or tenecteplase in the 4.5-hour thrombolytic treatment window, while emphasizing rapid treatment in eligible patients with disabling deficits regardless of NIHSS score within the 4.5-hour window without advanced imaging selection [N1-F1]. Another major change is the inclusion of pediatric patients. The 2026 guideline states that the guidelines include recommendations for interventional treatment in pediatric patients with AIS, although much work remains to adapt prehospital and hospital stroke protocols for pediatric patients [N1-F1]. The patient groups and settings emphasized in the current guidance are broad but especially focused on acute stroke care and secondary prevention. Core recommendations that have stayed the same include rapid treatment, standard of care for thrombolysis and endovascular therapy, and diagnostic evaluation for secondary prevention [N1-R2][N2-R2][N3-F2]. Acute stroke care updates and implementation details

The evidence shows a clear evolution in acute stroke care, especially around time windows, imaging eligibility, and team coordination. The 2026 Guideline for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke states that the guideline incorporates new evidence related to thrombolytic choice and eligibility, determination of eligibility for endovascular thrombectomy, and management of hyperglycemia and dysphagia [N1-F1]. It also reports that the guideline supports expanded use of endovascular thrombectomy and recommends either alteplase or tenecteplase in the 4.5-hour thrombolytic treatment window, with rapid treatment in eligible patients with disabling deficits regardless of NIHSS score within the 4.5-hour window without advanced imaging selection [N1-F1]. The guideline also supports extended window thrombolysis for select patients with stroke of unknown onset or 4.5–9 hours from onset using advanced imaging criteria such as diffusion-weighted imaging-fluid-attenuated inversion recovery or perfusion-based mismatch [N1-F1]. The Endovascular Therapy in Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke With ... guidelines provide focused practical recommendations based on recent evidence regarding selection and endovascular therapy [N2-R1]. The AHA/ASA focused update on endovascular therapy notes that patients with large vessel occlusion of the vertebral or basilar artery are now often treated with endovascular thrombectomy [N2-R5]. Taken together, these sources indicate that acute stroke care has moved from a more rigid time-window model toward a more flexible approach that combines standard IVT with extended eligibility criteria and expanded endovascular therapy.

For updated time windows for thrombolysis and endovascular therapy, the evidence is explicit. The 2026 guideline recommends alteplase or tenecteplase in the 4.5-hour thrombolytic treatment window [N1-F1]. It also supports extended window thrombolysis for select patients with stroke of unknown onset or 4.5–9 hours from onset using advanced imaging criteria [N1-F1]. The Endovascular Therapy guideline similarly focuses on selection and endovascular therapy in patients with acute ischemic stroke [N2-R1]. The AHA/ASA focused update emphasizes that EVT is recommended in patients with large vessel occlusion of the vertebral or basilar artery [N2-R5]. These findings show that IVT is still the mainstay of medical management, but the window is now more flexible and image-based for some patients [N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R5].

New imaging protocols or eligibility criteria are also central. The 2026 guideline specifically mentions determination of eligibility for endovascular thrombectomy, management of hyperglycemia and dysphagia, and the use of advanced imaging criteria for extended window thrombolysis [N1-F1]. The Endovascular Therapy guidelines summarize recent trials and key data in the treatment of patients with large ischemic core infarct, simplification of neuroimaging, and the role of advanced imaging [N2-R3]. The Stroke Systems of Care Framework materials emphasize that stroke systems should address training for hospital staff and support partnership development with hospitals, EMS agencies, and post-hospital organizations [N4-R1][N4-F3]. The evidence on stroke code and rapid response teams also shows that standardized protocols, teamwork, and interdisciplinary coordination are key to improving stroke care [N5-F4][N5-R4]. In addition, the Stroke Systems of Care resources include a hospital participation guide, a teamwork success story, and data collection tools, which imply that imaging and treatment decisions should be embedded in a coordinated systems approach rather than isolated clinical decisions [N4-F3].

Practical steps for rapid response and team coordination are strongly supported by the evidence. The 2026 guideline states that mobile stroke units enable rapid identification and treatment of thrombolytic-eligible patients with AIS, and that the guideline now includes recommendations related to the implementation of MSUs based on their safety and benefit [N1-F1]. It also endorses consideration of the characteristics of the local system of care and direct transport to the closest endovascular thrombectomy-capable hospital in the absence of well-functioning systems with rapid interhospital transfer processes [N1-F1]. The Stroke Code implementation study in the evidence reports that SC implementation in hospitals can improve the thrombolysis rate and shorten door-to-needle time [N5-F4]. The same study found that patients with RRT-initiated codes received imaging faster, with a mean time from code to imaging of 15.7 minutes compared with 23.2 minutes for non-RRT patients [N5-F4]. The Telestroke and stroke-code literature also emphasizes the importance of streamlining code stroke responses, implementing standardized protocols, and enhancing interdisciplinary teamwork [N5-R4]. The evidence-based practice implementation materials on stroke rehabilitation note barriers to implementation, including decreased resources such as staff, time, equipment, and training, as well as decreased communication among leadership [N4-R2]. Taken together, the practical steps for rapid response and team coordination include activating mobile stroke units, using local system-of-care characteristics to determine transport destination, implementing stroke code/RRT protocols, standardizing imaging and treatment workflows, and strengthening interdisciplinary communication and teamwork [N1-F1][N5-F4][N5-R4][N4-R2].

Overall, the acute stroke care updates indicate that IVT remains the standard of care, but eligibility has expanded to include some patients beyond 4.5 hours using advanced imaging criteria [N1-F1]. Endovascular therapy is now more broadly indicated, especially for large vessel occlusion and patients with large ischemic core infarct [N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R5]. Imaging protocols are becoming more image-driven, with diffusion-weighted imaging-fluid-attenuated inversion recovery or perfusion-based mismatch used to guide extended window thrombolysis [N1-F1][N2-R3]. The evidence indicates that common barriers to guideline implementation are operational, communication, and resource-related. The evidence-based practice implementation materials on stroke rehabilitation note that barriers to implementation include decreased resources such as staff, time, equipment, and training, as well as decreased communication among leadership [N4-R2]. The Stroke Systems of Care Framework materials also emphasize that stroke systems should address training for hospital staff and support partnership development with hospitals, EMS agencies, and post-hospital organizations [N4-R1][N4-F3]. The Stroke Code implementation study reports that SC implementation in hospitals can improve the thrombolysis rate and shorten door-to-needle time [N5-F4], suggesting that systems with poor coordination or delayed response can limit guideline uptake. The same study also found that patients with RRT-initiated codes received imaging faster, with a mean time from code to imaging of 15.7 minutes compared with 23.2 minutes for non-RRT patients [N5-F4], reinforcing that organizational delays can be a major barrier. The evidence on telestroke and code stroke also emphasizes the importance of streamlining code stroke responses, implementing standardized protocols, and enhancing interdisciplinary teamwork [N5-R4]. Taken together, the common barriers are delays in response, insufficient staffing and training, limited resources, poor communication, and weak coordination across care settings [N4-R2][N5-F4][N5-R4].

What training or staff education is recommended is directly tied to these barriers. The 2026 guideline states that stroke systems should address training for hospital staff [N4-R1][N4-F3]. The evidence-based practice implementation materials explicitly call for delivering stroke training to all hospital staff, including how to activate in-hospital stroke alerts and how to perform timely evaluations [N4-R5]. The Stroke Systems of Care Framework materials include training-focused resources such as a hospital participation guide, teamwork success stories, and a checklist for stroke alerts [N4-F3]. The Stroke Code implementation study also notes that stroke team members including nursing staff and supporting staff were trained on SC [N5-F4]. The evidence on rapid response teams adds that standardized protocols and interdisciplinary teamwork are needed to improve stroke care [N5-R4]. Therefore, recommended training should cover stroke recognition, activation of stroke alerts, rapid response protocols, teamwork, and use of systems-of-care tools [N4-R5][N4-F3][N5-F4][N5-R4]. Staff education should also include leadership communication and systems improvement, because decreased communication among leadership is a noted barrier [N4-R2].

Available systems-of-care frameworks and tools are substantial. In short, the main implementation barriers are decreased staff, time, equipment, training, and communication [N4-R2]. Recommended staff education includes stroke recognition, activation protocols, teamwork training, leadership communication, and systems improvement [N4-R5][N4-F3][N5-F4][N5-R4]. Available systems-of-care frameworks and tools include CDC stroke systems-of-care framework resources, a stroke program toolkit, hospital participation guides, partnership agreements, data collection and quality improvement tools, documentation tools, and community education materials [N4-R1][N4-R4][N4-R5][N4-F3].
